title: Ἄνθρωπος καὶ ἀλώπηξ
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 58. Text as printed. Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Ἀλώπεκά τις ἐχθρὰν ἔχων ὡς βλάπτουσαν αὐτόν, κρατήσας καὶ θέλων ἐπὶ πολὺ τιμωρήσασθαι, στυππεῖα ἐλαίῳ βεβρεγμένα τῇ οὐρᾷ προσδήσας ὑφῆψε.
sentences.tr: Alōpeka tis echthran echōn hōs blaptousan auton, kratēsas kai thelōn epi poly timōrēsasthai, styppeia elaiōi bebregmena tēi ourāi prosdēsas hyphēpse.
sentences.l: Someone, having a fox as an enemy on the ground that she was harming him, having-caught her and wishing to take vengeance at length, having-tied tow soaked in oil to her tail, set it alight.
sentences.i: A man who counted a fox his enemy because she was doing him harm caught her, and, wishing to punish her long and thoroughly, tied tow soaked in oil to her tail and set it on fire.
sentences.n: ὡς with the participle (ὡς βλάπτουσαν) gives the ground as the man himself sees it — 'on the ground that she was harming him'. στυππεῖα is coarse flax fibre, tow, which catches fire instantly. ἐπὶ πολύ is 'over a long stretch', of how far the punishment was to go.

sentences.t: Ταύτην δὲ δαίμων εἰς τὰς ἀρούρας τοῦ βαλόντος ὡδήγει· ἦν δὲ καιρὸς τοῦ ἀμήτου.
sentences.tr: Tautēn de daimōn eis tas arouras tou balontos hōdēgei· ēn de kairos tou amētou.
sentences.l: But a divinity was leading her into the fields of the man who had thrown the fire; and it was the season of the harvest.
sentences.n: δαίμων here is not a demon but an unnamed divine power — the fable's way of saying that what followed was more than chance. τοῦ βαλόντος is an aorist participle used as a noun, 'of the one who had thrown (the fire)'. ἄμητος is the reaping of the standing grain.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἠκολούθει θρηνῶν μηδὲν θερίσας.
sentences.tr: Ho de ēkolouthei thrēnōn mēden therisas.
sentences.l: And he followed, lamenting, having reaped nothing.
sentences.n: Ὁ δέ, 'and he', is the article doing duty as a pronoun to swing the subject back to the man — constant in these fables. The negative with the participle is μηδέν, not οὐδέν: in the Greek of these collections μή has largely displaced οὐ with the participle, even where the statement is one of plain fact.

sentences.t: Ὅτι πρᾷον εἶναι χρὴ καὶ μὴ ἀμέτρως θυμοῦσθαι· ἐξ ὀργῆς γὰρ πολλάκις βλάβη γίνεται μεγάλη τοῖς δυσοργήτοις.
sentences.tr: Hoti prāion einai chrē kai mē ametrōs thymousthai· ex orgēs gar pollakis blabē ginetai megalē tois dysorgētois.
sentences.l: That one must be gentle and not be angry beyond measure; for out of anger great harm often comes to the hot-tempered.
sentences.n: A bare Ὅτι moral: the 'the story shows' is unexpressed in the Greek, which opens simply 'That…'. χρή takes a plain infinitive with no expressed subject, 'one must'. δυσόργητος is 'hard to handle in anger', quick to rage and slow to cool.
